supported_facts: The New York Times reported that five people with knowledge of the discussions said Kushner had spoken with potential investors about raising $5 billion or more for Affinity Partners while serving as a U.S. Middle East negotiator; it also reported that Affinity representatives met with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, an existing $2 billion investor.

The March 19 Garcia-Wyden letter said it 'appears' Kushner was seeking at least $5 billion while representing the U.S. in Middle East negotiations and requested information to investigate potential conflicts.
Bloomberg reported, based on a regulatory filing, that Affinity's assets reached $6.2 billion at year-end 2025; it said gains on investments contributed to the increase.
unsupported_original_claims: The $5 billion target was directed exclusively to Saudi Arabia.
A quid pro quo between Saudi investment and Kushner's diplomatic role occurred.
Affinity had $6.1 billion in assets or 99% foreign-owned assets; the cited Bloomberg figure is $6.2 billion in assets, not a finding of 99% foreign ownership.
The cited reporting establishes that Kushner's diplomatic role was unpaid or that he was exempt from federal financial-disclosure requirements.
access_notes: The NYT page returned HTTP 403 to direct retrieval; its article text was read through an Exa citation tied to the exact URL. The House letter PDF text was extracted through Exa. Bloomberg's exact article was retrieved with Firecrawl. The congressional letter's statements are lawmakers' concerns and requests, not independent findings.

source_evidence.evidence_excerpt: Kushner had spoken with potential investors about raising '$5 billion or more' for Affinity, according to five people with knowledge; Affinity representatives had met with Saudi PIF.
source_evidence.supports: Fundraising target, investor meeting, and simultaneous diplomatic role; target is not capital actually raised.
source_evidence.access: Exact article text returned by Exa; direct URL fetch returned 403.

source_evidence.evidence_excerpt: The letter says it 'appears' Kushner is seeking 'at least $5 billion' while representing the U.S. in Middle East negotiations, then requests information.
source_evidence.supports: Congressional scrutiny and request for information; the letter is not an adjudicated or independently established finding.

source_evidence.evidence_excerpt: Bloomberg says a regulatory filing showed Affinity assets at $6.2 billion at end of 2025 and attributes the increase partly to investment gains.
source_evidence.supports: Reported assets figure only; it does not establish 99% foreign ownership or the new fundraising target.

uncertainty_note: The $5 billion is a fundraising target reported by unnamed sources, not money confirmed as received. The NYT says other regional investors were being approached and that PIF was an existing major investor; no source establishes Saudi Arabia alone was solicited or that diplomacy and investment were exchanged. The congressional letter raises concerns rather than proving them.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Kushner Seeks a New Affinity Fund While Participating in Middle East Diplomacy
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: The New York Times reported that Jared Kushner discussed raising $5 billion or more for Affinity Partners while participating in U.S. Middle East diplomacy; it also reported that Affinity representatives met with Saudi Arabia's existing $2 billion investor, PIF. A congressional letter sought details and raised conflict concerns. The reporting establishes a fundraising target and overlap, not a quid pro quo.

support_note: The NYT article text directly reports a $5 billion-or-more fundraising target, attributed to five people with knowledge, and identifies Kushner as a U.S. Middle East negotiator; it says Affinity representatives met with Saudi PIF. The Garcia-Wyden letter repeats the target as an appearance and asks for records, so it supports that scrutiny was raised, not that a conflict or exchange was proved. Bloomberg's filing-based report supports the separate $6.2 billion year-end asset figure.

supported_facts: CBO's October 28, 2025 cost estimate for the enacted Medicaid chapter of P.L. 119-21 says CBO and JCT estimate the provisions would increase the number of people without health insurance by 7.5 million in 2034.
CRS report R48633 says the law's broader health-coverage provisions are estimated to increase the uninsured population by 10.0 million in FY2034 relative to CBO's January 2025 baseline.
unsupported_original_claims: The 10.0 million estimate for all health-coverage provisions is attributable only to Medicaid.
The enacted law's Medicaid effect is interchangeable with the House-passed bill's estimate.
access_notes: CBO publication 61837 was retrieved with Firecrawl and CRS report R48633 was retrieved from EveryCRSReport; the full report text distinguishes Medicaid provisions from broader health-coverage provisions.

source_evidence.evidence_excerpt: CBO and JCT estimate the combined effects of the Medicaid chapter will increase the number of people without health insurance by '7.5 million in 2034.'
source_evidence.supports: The enacted Medicaid provisions' projected uninsured effect.
source_evidence.access: Exact CBO page retrieved with Firecrawl; page identifies estimate as for P.L. 119-21 as enacted July 4, 2025.

source_evidence.evidence_excerpt: CRS says the health-coverage provisions in the reconciliation law increase the number without insurance by '10.0 million in FY2034'; it separately identifies 7.5 million for Medicaid.
source_evidence.supports: Distinguishes the broader law-wide coverage estimate from the Medicaid-specific estimate.

uncertainty_note: Both figures are CBO projections for 2034 relative to the stated baseline, not observed counts. The 10.0 million figure covers broader health-coverage provisions and must not be labeled Medicaid-only.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: CBO Estimates Medicaid Provisions Add 7.5 Million Uninsured by 2034
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: CBO estimated that the Medicaid chapter of the enacted 2025 reconciliation law would leave 7.5 million more people uninsured in 2034. CRS separately reports a 10.0 million increase from the law's broader health-coverage provisions; the estimates have different scopes and are projections, not observed losses.

support_note: CBO publication 61837 is a cost estimate for the enacted Medicaid chapter and explicitly says the combined provisions increase the uninsured by 7.5 million in 2034. CRS R48633 separately reports 10.0 million for the broader health-coverage provisions. These are projections against a baseline, not observed coverage losses.

supported_facts: MS NOW reports that Wilkins had a detail made up of elite FBI agents usually assigned to a SWAT team in the Nashville field office; the FBI said the detail was due to hundreds of credible death threats.

The Seattle Times reports that SWAT agents escorted Wilkins to a Nashville hair-salon appointment, to appearances and errands, and on travel including a British resort before dinner at Windsor Castle; those accounts are attributed to sources.

The Seattle Times reports, citing an FBI official briefed on plans, that a four-agent, two-vehicle detail was assigned and that Patel overrode advice to conduct a legal review. It also quotes an FBI spokesperson later saying Wilkins faced more than a dozen active death threats, while noting an earlier statement had put the number in the hundreds.
unsupported_original_claims: The detail's purpose was to support Wilkins's music career; the FBI attributed protection to threats, although reporting says agents accompanied her to performances and personal errands.
The reported staffing plan and Patel's alleged instruction are established by official records or independently adjudicated findings; the Seattle Times attributes them to sources.
access_notes: MS NOW's exact article was retrieved directly; the Seattle Times page was extracted with Firecrawl. Both outlets attribute operational details to sources, and the FBI's stated threat rationale is separately attributed to a spokesperson.

source_evidence.evidence_excerpt: Wilkins's detail was made up of elite FBI agents usually assigned to the Nashville SWAT team; the FBI said she faced 'hundreds of credible death threats.'
source_evidence.supports: Existence and reported staffing of the security detail, and the FBI's stated rationale.
source_evidence.access: Exact article retrieved directly; source quote is attributed to the FBI.

source_evidence.evidence_excerpt: The report describes a hair-salon escort, a trip before Windsor Castle dinner, singing appearances and errands; it attributes four agents/two vehicles and Patel's legal-review direction to sources.
source_evidence.supports: Specific escort and staffing allegations as reported, not as independently verified official records.
source_evidence.access: Exact article extracted with Firecrawl. The FBI spokesperson quoted in the article cited more than a dozen active threats and an earlier count in the hundreds.

uncertainty_note: The details about errands, staffing, and Patel's directions rest on anonymous or unnamed sources, not operational records in the cited articles. The FBI spokesperson's threat counts differ by time and wording; the articles do not establish that music work, rather than threat protection, was the official purpose of the detail.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: FBI SWAT Detail Protected Alexis Wilkins; Reports Describe Escorts to Events and Errands
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: MS NOW reported that the FBI provided Alexis Wilkins a Nashville-based detail staffed by agents usually assigned to SWAT and quoted the FBI citing hundreds of credible death threats. The Seattle Times separately reported escorts to a salon, performances, errands and travel, plus a four-agent/two-vehicle plan and Patel's direction, based on sources. Those operational allegations are attributed reporting, not independently verified records.

exact_gap: No operational logs or legal-review records are included in the cited sources to independently verify the reported escorts, staffing arrangement, or Patel's alleged direction.
support_note: MS NOW's article says the detail consisted of elite agents usually assigned to Nashville SWAT and quotes the FBI citing 'hundreds of credible death threats.' The Seattle Times separately reports specific escorts and staffing/command allegations, attributing them to unnamed people and an FBI official briefed on plans. Its spokesperson quote gives a later count of more than a dozen active threats and notes an earlier 'hundreds' statement.

supported_facts: Gallup reported that 40% of Americans approved of Trump's overall job performance in its August 1–20, 2025 poll.
Gallup said support was in line with June and July.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited poll found 29% approval or a historic low for second-term presidents.
The article text retrieved for this URL does not show a 56% disapproval result, so that figure is not relied upon in this outcome.
access_notes: Gallup's exact article was retrieved directly and its survey-method section reviewed; it reports interviews Aug. 1–20, 2025, of 1,094 adults and a ±4-point margin of sampling error.

source_evidence.evidence_excerpt: The article says '40% of Americans' approved of Trump's overall job performance, 'in line with support for him in June and July'; its survey-method section gives Aug. 1–20, 2025, n=1,094, margin ±4 points.
source_evidence.supports: The approval figure, field dates, comparison with June/July, and poll limits.

uncertainty_note: This is a survey estimate with a ±4-point margin of sampling error, not an exact count. The retrieved article supports 40% approval but does not substantiate the 29% claim, a historic-low comparison, or the prior row's 56% disapproval figure.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Gallup Found 40% Approval for Trump in Its August 2025 Poll
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: Gallup reported 40% approval of Trump's overall job performance in its Aug. 1–20, 2025 survey and said the rating was in line with June and July. The poll interviewed 1,094 adults with a ±4-point margin of sampling error; this source does not support a 29% historic low.

exact_gap: The 56% disapproval figure was not present in the text of the cited Gallup article and is not used here.
support_note: Gallup's August 26 article says 40% approved of Trump's overall job performance and describes it as in line with June and July. The method section dates interviews Aug. 1–20, 2025, with 1,094 adults and a ±4 percentage-point margin of sampling error.

supported_facts: CBO publication 61510 estimates that the Medicaid provisions in title IV of H.R. 1, as passed by the House on May 22, 2025, would increase the number of people without health insurance by 7.8 million in 2034 relative to current-law baseline projections.

CBO publication 61461 is the June 4, 2025 estimate of H.R. 1's overall budgetary effects as passed by the House; the consulted page and summary workbook show estimates by title, not a directly stated Medicaid-only $793 billion figure.
unsupported_original_claims: The $793 billion Medicaid-only reduction is directly established by the two cited publications; that exact Medicaid-only amount was not located in their retrieved source text.
The original $880 billion and 8.6 million figures are not the matching CBO estimate in publication 61510.
The 'largest transfer of wealth' superlative is an established CBO finding.
access_notes: CBO publication pages 61510 and 61461 were retrieved with Firecrawl; the downloadable 61461 summary workbook was also extracted. Publication 61510 directly states the 7.8 million Medicaid-coverage estimate. The 61461 summary is a bill-level budget estimate; no Medicaid-only $793 billion statement was located.

source_evidence.evidence_excerpt: CBO estimates that the Medicaid provisions in title IV of H.R. 1 would increase the number without health insurance by '7.8 million in 2034' relative to current-law baseline; the page identifies the bill as passed by the House May 22, 2025.
source_evidence.supports: The narrower Medicaid coverage estimate for the House-passed version.
source_evidence.access: Exact CBO page and linked letter retrieved with Firecrawl.

source_evidence.evidence_excerpt: The page is titled 'Estimated Budgetary Effects of H.R. 1' and identifies the version as passed by the House May 22, 2025; its downloadable summary workbook tabulates bill effects by title.
source_evidence.supports: Version and overall budget scoring, not the $793 billion Medicaid-only amount.
source_evidence.access: Page and linked workbook summary retrieved with Firecrawl; no Medicaid-only $793 billion statement located in the consulted text.

uncertainty_note: The 7.8 million figure is a CBO projection for 2034 relative to a current-law baseline. The $793 billion Medicaid-only reduction needs a source that explicitly isolates that amount for the House-passed version; the two cited CBO sources consulted here do not do so.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: CBO Projected 7.8 Million More Uninsured From House-Passed H.R. 1 Medicaid Provisions
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: CBO estimated that Medicaid provisions in the House-passed H.R. 1 would increase the number of people without insurance by 7.8 million in 2034 relative to current-law projections. The cited CBO sources do not directly substantiate a $793 billion Medicaid-only total, so that figure is omitted.

exact_gap: A CBO source explicitly isolating the House-passed bill's 10-year Medicaid-only spending reduction is needed to support the $793 billion figure.
support_note: CBO publication 61510 directly states that title IV Medicaid provisions in the House-passed bill were estimated to add 7.8 million people without insurance by 2034. Publication 61461 identifies the version and presents the bill's overall estimated budgetary effects; its consulted summary does not directly establish the $793 billion Medicaid-only amount. The defensible correction retains the coverage estimate and drops that unverified spending figure.

supported_facts: EPA's March 12, 2025 release says Zeldin announced updated enforcement discretion and immediate revisions to National Enforcement and Compliance Initiatives, including a direction to focus on pressing health and safety issues and not shut down energy production.
EPA separately reported on February 11 that 171 DEIA and environmental-justice employees were placed on administrative leave (11 and 160, respectively).
EPA separately reported on March 10 that it canceled more than 400 grants across nine programs totaling $1.7 billion.
unsupported_original_claims: One February event dismantled all clean-air and clean-water enforcement divisions.
The cited releases establish that all industrial-polluter investigations stopped or that air and drinking-water standards were withdrawn.
Campaign donations caused these agency actions or led to a specific increase in pollution.
access_notes: All three exact EPA press releases were retrieved directly; the actions occurred in separate releases dated February 11, March 10, and March 12, 2025.

source_evidence.evidence_excerpt: March 12 release: Zeldin announced 'updated enforcement discretion' and revisions to National Enforcement and Compliance Initiatives, focused on stated core mission and pressing health/safety issues.
source_evidence.supports: A discrete change in enforcement priorities on March 12, 2025.

source_evidence.evidence_excerpt: February 11 release says 171 DEIA and Environmental Justice employees were placed on administrative leave, split 11 and 160.
March 10 release says more than 400 grants across nine programs, totaling $1.7 billion, were canceled.

uncertainty_note: These are EPA's own press releases, so they document announced agency actions and its framing, not independently measured enforcement outcomes. They do not identify every affected program or establish that all clean-air/clean-water enforcement ended.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Zeldin EPA Reprioritizes Enforcement and Announces Separate Staffing and Grant Actions
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: On March 12, 2025, Lee Zeldin announced updated EPA enforcement discretion and revisions to enforcement priorities. Separate EPA releases reported 171 DEIA and Environmental Justice employees placed on leave on February 11 and more than 400 grants canceled on March 10. These releases document specific changes, not a wholesale end to clean-air and clean-water enforcement.

exact_gap: Program-level records would be needed to establish the scope of enforcement changes or effects on particular air- and water-pollution investigations.
support_note: EPA's own March 12 release directly describes updated enforcement discretion and revisions to enforcement priorities. Its February 11 employee-leave release and March 10 grant-cancellation release support separate administrative actions, not a single shutdown of air- and water-enforcement divisions. These are the agency's announcements and characterizations.

supported_facts: Executive Order 14243, signed March 20, 2025, directs designated federal officials to obtain full and prompt access to unclassified agency records, data, and systems for waste, fraud, and abuse work, to the maximum extent consistent with law.

The order directs review of agency guidance and regulations governing unclassified data access, including system-of-records notices; it specifically addresses data from federally funded state programs and unemployment records.
Section 4 says the order must be implemented consistent with applicable law.
unsupported_original_claims: The order was signed in February.
It expressly repealed the Privacy Act or independently authorized unrestricted access to all tax, health, immigration, and law-enforcement files.
The order itself created a comprehensive national surveillance database.
access_notes: The exact White House executive-order text was retrieved directly; its provisions and general-law limitation were read.

source_evidence.evidence_excerpt: Section 3(a) directs full and prompt access to unclassified records/data/systems 'to the maximum extent consistent with law'; Section 3(b) calls for review of regulations including system-of-records notices; Section 4(b) says implementation must be consistent with applicable law.
source_evidence.supports: The order's data-sharing direction, its review of access rules, and its express legal limitation.
source_evidence.access: Exact White House order text retrieved directly.

uncertainty_note: The order's broad access and review directives raise implementation questions, but its text does not itself show which protected records were accessed or establish a national database. It does not mention the Privacy Act by name; the 'consistent with law' clauses do not by themselves resolve every downstream privacy question.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Trump Orders Broader Lawful Sharing of Unclassified Federal Data
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: Executive Order 14243, signed March 20, 2025, directs agencies to expand officials' access to unclassified data for waste, fraud, and abuse work and to review rules that impede sharing. It requires implementation consistent with law; its text does not itself repeal the Privacy Act or establish a comprehensive surveillance database.

exact_gap: Agency implementation records are needed to determine access to particular protected records and the practical effect on privacy safeguards.
support_note: The order's Section 3(a) directs access to unclassified agency records, systems, and data for waste/fraud/abuse work and authorizes intra- and inter-agency sharing; Sections 3(b) and 4 require actions to remain, to the stated extent, consistent with law. The order reviews system-of-records notices but does not name or repeal the Privacy Act.
